title: Finish the Artifact with Evidence and Revision
learner_promise: Finish your continuing project within its approved scope, demonstrate a meaningful correction with retest evidence, and explain the honest limits of the completed result.
outcomes: Compare the artifact with the approved FOCUS charter and original success criteria.
Use BUILD to plan and lead a bounded material revision.
Test ordinary use and known exceptions, then retest the correction.
Save the finished artifact, evidence trail, and scope reconciliation with accurate limits.

teaching.heading: Return to the charter and preserve the baseline
paragraphs: A finished project begins with the purpose you already approved. Bring forward your FOCUS charter and the success criteria you wrote earlier. Your charter names the bounded result you intend to make. Your success criteria describe what must be true for that result to be useful. Today, compare those criteria with the artifact you can actually open, show, or use. Your capstone is the completed version of this continuing project. It does not need to become a larger project to become a stronger one.

Start by preserving a baseline. A baseline is the version you will compare with your revised work. Give it a meaningful name or version identifier and retain the relevant inputs and test observations. If you overwrite the only copy, you may lose the evidence that explains what improved. Keep private or sensitive information out of any example you share with AI. Use permitted references, remove identifying details where needed, and label recreated or fictional material accurately.

For each success criterion, ask three practical questions. What does the charter require? What can the current artifact demonstrate? What evidence supports that answer? A requirement may be met, unmet, or not yet established. Those answers are different. If you have not tested a requirement, mark the evidence as missing. Do not call it passed because the screen looks polished or because AI says the design should work. A clear comparison helps you choose the next correction.

Our worked example is a supplied fictional intake exercise. Its charter promises a reviewed intake process. The criteria require complete input to reach a named human reviewer, missing information to remain visible, and delivery to wait for human approval. The first draft takes intake details and prepares an output, but it does not include a reliable approval gate. A dashboard showing the number of records would be outside the correction needed here. It would not establish that approval happens before delivery.

Make the remaining work small enough to inspect. Choose the unmet criterion with the greatest consequence for the intended use. Write a staged plan: complete the missing step, review its behavior, test the ordinary path, and test a known exception. Define what evidence you will keep at each stage. If the missing step cannot be completed within the agreed scope, record the limit and revisit the completion claim. A limitation that breaks a core success criterion cannot be hidden in a footnote.

Pause and open your own charter. Name the current version, one criterion you can already support, and one evidence gap that needs attention. Keep this comparison in your Project Record and workbook. You will use it to lead the revision rather than ask AI to decide what your project should become.
teaching.think_prompt: Which criterion is supported, unmet, or not yet established in your current version?

teaching.heading: Use BUILD to lead a bounded revision
paragraphs: BUILD gives you a practical sequence for completing your artifact: baseline, use AI, inspect, lead, and demonstrate. Baseline means preserving the starting version and its observed behavior. Use AI means asking for help with the approved task using appropriate inputs. Inspect means checking the proposed output against your charter, evidence, and intended use. Lead means making the human decision about what to change. Demonstrate means showing the revised result and the evidence that supports it.

Use the approved request in this lesson. It asks AI to check the artifact against the charter and success criteria, identify missing evidence and defects before suggesting additions, and help prioritize a bounded revision. Supply a privacy-safe representation of your artifact and actual test notes. Include the relevant criteria so the review has a clear reference. Do not supply a confidential record merely because it would be convenient. Keep the request and the useful output with the version you reviewed.

An AI suggestion is a candidate for inspection. It may identify a real gap, misunderstand the purpose, or propose extra features. You remain responsible for comparing it with the record. Ask which criterion each proposed change serves. Ask whether the change is needed for the current result or belongs outside the present scope. If a suggestion depends on access, permission, or a capability you do not have, record that dependency. Do not describe a proposed connection as a working integration.

In the fictional intake example, a useful correction is an explicit review state and approval gate. An incomplete intake remains pending and identifies the missing delivery date. A complete intake becomes a draft for the named reviewer. Approval must be recorded before the process permits delivery. If approval is absent, the output stays unapproved. These are intended behaviors in a tabletop design. They are not evidence that a live system has been deployed or that a real customer has received anything.

A material revision changes something that matters to the success criteria. Correcting an invented date, repairing the approval step, or making an exception visible can be material. Changing a heading may improve readability, but it does not by itself repair a failed approval criterion. Keep the before and after versions and explain the consequence of the change. That explanation should identify the defect, the decision, and the behavior you expect the correction to produce.

Write the remaining build, review, and testing steps in order. Decide who makes the human decision and what evidence will show that it happened. You may use real human feedback or criteria-based feedback. Criteria-based feedback means a documented comparison with stated criteria; it does not mean another person approved the work. Label the method honestly. Now select one correction for your own artifact. Explain why it is inside the charter and why the tempting additions can wait.
teaching.think_prompt: Which correction serves the charter, and which proposed addition can wait?

teaching.heading: Test ordinary use, exceptions, and the correction
paragraphs: A realistic test uses inputs and conditions that matter to the intended use of your artifact. It is more useful than a demonstration that only works with perfect information. Begin with the ordinary path: the situation your project is meant to handle most often. Write the input, expected behavior, observed behavior, and result. Keep a reference to the version you tested. If your artifact is a document, the test may be a reader task or a criteria review. If it is a workflow or prototype, the test may be a safe walkthrough. Describe the method you actually used.

Then test a known exception. Choose a condition you identified in earlier journey work, such as a missing input, an ambiguous instruction, or a required approval that has not occurred. State what responsible handling would look like. Your artifact should not quietly invent information or continue through a decision that belongs to a person. A test result is not just pass or fail. It should explain what happened and point to evidence another person can inspect.

Our supplied fictional case has three tabletop tests. In the ordinary case, the delivery date is present and the completed intake reaches the named reviewer as a draft. In the missing-input case, the delivery date is absent; the process stays pending and asks for that date. In the approval exception, the input is complete but the reviewer has not approved it; delivery remains blocked. These observations are supplied for teaching. Run and record your own tests rather than copy them as your results.

The baseline first draft fails the approval exception because it treats a completed draft as ready to deliver. The human correction separates complete input from approved output. A material correction therefore needs a retest. A retest is a repeat check after the change, using the relevant conditions again. Run the approval exception on the revised version. Also rerun the ordinary and missing-input cases to check that the correction has not damaged them. Keep the revised output and the observation for each case.

Obtain feedback using a method you can describe accurately. If a person reviews the work, record their relevant comment and your response, with permission where necessary. If you use criteria-based feedback, record the criterion, the comparison, and the gap found. AI can help organize that review, but an AI response is not human approval. Identify which suggestions you accepted, which you declined, and why.

Compare the baseline with the retested version. Claim only the improvement the comparison supports. In the teaching example, the revised tabletop now retains an unapproved state until human approval is recorded. That does not establish live reliability, measured time savings, or customer benefit. For your own project, choose a specific claim and open the evidence beside it. If the correction still fails, keep the result pending and continue the bounded repair before claiming completion.
teaching.think_prompt: What changed in the relevant retest, and where can you show the evidence?

teaching.heading: Reconcile the scope and save the finished result
paragraphs: Finishing the artifact means bringing the result, the charter, and the evidence into agreement. Scope reconciliation is that final comparison. It explains what you promised, what you completed, what the evidence supports, and what remains outside the current result. Keep those points together so a reviewer does not have to guess whether a feature is working, proposed, or unavailable. A complete bounded artifact can have visible limits that are consistent with its intended use.

Start with the core success criteria. Point to the current artifact and a meaningful evidence reference for each one. Include the ordinary test and known exceptions. Include the before and after correction and its retest. If a required behavior still lacks evidence, say so and resolve it before treating that criterion as satisfied. Do not redefine the original purpose simply to make an incomplete result appear finished. Any material scope change needs an honest explanation and appropriate review.

Next, record what remains outside scope. In the fictional intake case, the reviewed tabletop demonstrates the planned handling of complete inputs, missing dates, and absent approval. It has not established live delivery, real system integration, production reliability, or measured benefit. A new dashboard is outside the present charter. These limits keep the completion claim precise. They do not excuse an approval step that still fails. The distinction is whether the remaining limit is compatible with the result you promised.

Save the finished artifact with meaningful sources and version identifiers. Your evidence trail should preserve the useful requests, outputs, tests, feedback, and human decisions that explain the work. You do not need a pile of every discarded output. You do need the record that makes the material correction understandable. Keep private information protected, retain permitted originals where appropriate, and label any sanitized or recreated illustration. An illustration is not the original record of a result.

Complete the matching workbook section. Record the baseline and current version, success criteria, staged BUILD plan, actual test observations, feedback method, before and after revision, retest result, scope limits, and evidence index. Save this work in the Capstone Integration Package of your continuing Project Record. Earlier evidence remains part of the same project. The workbook gives you a place to organize your explanation; it does not replace the finished artifact or its supporting records.

Now do the applied completion check. Show the finished result and a before-and-after correction. Explain why the artifact satisfies the charter and what it has not yet established. A useful answer points to visible work, describes your judgment, and stays within the evidence. Carry this package into Lesson Six Point Three for the quality, responsibility, and readiness review. During the journey's independent work, strengthen weak evidence and rehearse your demonstration using the same project. AI assists. Humans verify.
teaching.think_prompt: What does your completed result establish, and what remains outside scope?

worked_case.label: Repair the approval step before adding a dashboard
worked_case.setup: SUPPLIED FICTIONAL TRAINING CASE: A reviewed intake process must handle complete input, a missing delivery date, and absent human approval. The baseline produces a draft but treats completed input as permission to deliver. No live system, real customer, actual delivery, or measured benefit is demonstrated. The following tabletop observations are supplied for teaching; your project requires your own tests.

evidence_table.claim: A complete draft is ready to deliver.
evidence_table.evidence: The baseline has complete input but no recorded human approval.
evidence_table.action: Mark the approval criterion unmet; keep the draft unapproved.

evidence_table.claim: A dashboard will finish the project.
evidence_table.evidence: Counting records does not demonstrate missing-input handling or approval.
evidence_table.action: Defer the addition and repair the required gate.

evidence_table.claim: The revised tabletop satisfies the reviewed intake criteria.
evidence_table.evidence: Supplied revised observations: complete intake reaches reviewer; missing date remains pending; absent approval blocks delivery.
evidence_table.action: Retain the before/after versions and retest all three cases.

evidence_table.claim: The work improves live operations and saves time.
evidence_table.evidence: Only fictional tabletop observations are supplied; there is no live deployment or measurement.
evidence_table.action: Limit the claim to the reviewed tabletop and identify unestablished outcomes.

worked_case.revised_example: Version 2: Incomplete intake stays pending with the missing date identified. Complete intake becomes a draft for the named human reviewer. Without recorded approval, delivery remains blocked. The revised fictional tabletop demonstrates these three paths; it does not establish live delivery, integration, reliability, or measured benefit.
demonstration_steps: Preserve Version 1 and compare it with the three charter criteria.
Use AI to propose the approval correction; inspect it and record the human decision.
Keep Version 2 and retest complete input, missing date, and absent approval.
Save the evidence references and scope limits; defer the dashboard.
worked_case.question: Which before-and-after observation proves the approval correction, and which claim remains unestablished?

application.heading: Preserve and compare the baseline
application.instruction: Open the same project, approved charter, success criteria, and current artifact. Preserve the baseline with a meaningful identifier. Mark each criterion supported, unmet, or not yet established.
application.evidence: Baseline reference, criterion comparison, and priority gap.

application.heading: Lead the bounded BUILD correction
application.instruction: Plan the remaining build, review, and tests. Use the approved AI request with privacy-safe artifact and test inputs. Inspect the response and make one material revision that serves the charter.
application.evidence: Staged BUILD plan, meaningful AI request/output, human decision, and before/after versions.

application.heading: Test, obtain feedback, and retest
application.instruction: Run a realistic ordinary test and known exception. Obtain actual human or criteria-based feedback, naming the method accurately. Retest the material correction and check the other paths for unintended changes.
application.evidence: Inputs, expected and observed behavior, results, feedback, and revised-version retest.

application.heading: Finish and reconcile the scope
application.instruction: Save the current artifact, compare it with the baseline, and identify completed requirements and outside-scope work. Complete the workbook and save the evidence in your Capstone Integration Package.
application.evidence: Finished artifact reference, evidence trail, scope reconciliation, and honest limits.

approved_ai_request: Check this artifact against the approved charter and success criteria. Identify missing evidence and defects before suggesting additions. Help prioritize a bounded revision. Inputs: [artifact and tests].
responsibility_map_fields: AI input permission and useful request/output
Named human decision and feedback method
Ordinary and exception tests with version references
Material correction, retest, and evidence-supported claim
Remaining limits, outside-scope work, and next review

verification.heading: Show the result and correction
verification.prompt: Show the finished result and a before-and-after correction. Explain why the artifact satisfies the charter and what it has not yet established.

verification.heading: Check the improvement claim
verification.prompt: Open the baseline and revised-version retest. Does the observed change support the stated improvement? Keep untested or failed requirements pending.

verification.heading: Check the saved evidence and scope
verification.prompt: Open the finished artifact, meaningful sources, requests, outputs, tests, feedback, decisions, and version identifiers. Are the limits visible and consistent with intended use?

completion_criteria: The same project is compared with its original charter and success criteria.
The baseline and finished artifact can be opened through meaningful references.
A material before-and-after correction is explained and retested.
Ordinary use and known exceptions have actual recorded observations.
Feedback is labeled as human or criteria-based accurately.
Evidence-supported claims and outside-scope or unestablished outcomes are explicit.
The evidence trail and scope reconciliation are saved in the Capstone Integration Package and workbook.
handoff: Carry the finished artifact, correction and retest evidence, scope reconciliation, and remaining limits into Lesson 6.3 — Complete the Quality, Responsibility and Readiness Review. Strengthen weak evidence during the journey’s independent work using the same project.

media_transcripts.introduction: Welcome to Journey Six, Lesson Two: Finish the Artifact with Evidence and Revision. You already have a purpose for your project. Today, you will turn that purpose into a finished result you can show and explain. Start with your approved charter. What did you promise to make? Who is it for? What would count as a useful result? Compare your current work with those original success criteria before you ask AI to add anything. A polished appearance does not prove that the important steps work. In our fictional intake example, a new dashboard cannot repair a missing human approval step. You will use BUILD: baseline, use AI, inspect, lead, and demonstrate. Keep the version you started with, test the ordinary path and a known exception, collect honest feedback, and make one material correction. Then test that correction again. Save the finished artifact, the before and after evidence, and a clear account of what remains outside your scope. You do not have to claim perfection. You do need to show what works, what changed, and what your evidence actually supports. The evidence trail is the record of your sources, requests, outputs, tests, feedback, and decisions. Keep meaningful version names so another person can follow the correction without guessing. Open your workbook, bring forward your charter, and let us finish the work with care.
